claims.text: A machine-learning-based parameter optimization framework can be integrated with spark plasma sintering.
ML-optimized SPS can substantially reduce the temperature required to densify powder-based materials.
The proposed temperature reduction can be achieved while preserving mechanical properties.
Metallic powder feedstock can be consolidated by SPS into bulk material.
Ceramic powder feedstock can be consolidated by SPS.
A data-driven model can predict optimal SPS temperature, pressure, and time.
Applying model-predicted SPS parameters enables densification at lower temperatures.
The optimized SPS process can operate at a peak temperature at least 200 °C below conventional sintering.
Controlled dwell time, moderate pressure, and iterative model-guided adjustment support lower-temperature SPS densification.
Pulsed DC current in SPS accelerates mass transfer at particle contacts.
ML-identified parameter sets augment SPS densification mechanisms at lower temperatures.
Localized heating and rapid sintering under pulsed current are more efficient than conventional furnace heating.
Data-driven parameter selection can identify conditions under which diffusion is sufficient for consolidation below typical sintering temperatures.
ML-optimized SPS will achieve near-complete densification at temperatures at least 200 °C below standard protocols.
ML-optimized lower-temperature SPS will cause little or no loss of mechanical integrity.
Traditional furnace sintering or unoptimized SPS typically requires peak temperatures of at least 1600 °C to obtain comparable density and microstructure.
The attainable reduction in sintering temperature depends on material composition.
The attainable temperature reduction depends on the availability of robust experimental data for ML training.
Temperature reduction and mechanical-property retention vary with feedstock chemistry and parameter constraints.

contradictions.description: The conditions and predicted outcome define success as a temperature reduction of at least 200 °C, whereas the falsification rule describes a reduction of ≤200 °C as failure. At exactly 200 °C, the success and failure criteria overlap, and the inequality in the falsification rule may be reversed.
